clue.text: Organ friction? Possibly something for you to put on here in the mag.

definitions.text: something for you to put on

parts.note: the organ of sight
wear is the damage friction does over time
surface padding: a wink at the magazine's own title, Private Eye

explanation.surface: A puzzling bit of rubbing, then a nudge that the magazine you are holding has something to put on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' and 'here in the mag' wink at the magazine's own title, Private Eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasses and goggles are clothing-style items worn over the face, so they are things a reader might put on.

clue.text: It's rough backing Straw and Balls

indicators.note: backing means moving in reverse, so the word for straw is written backwards

parts.note: hay is dried grass, similar to straw; reversed it reads YAH
two balls look like the letter O twice

explanation.surface: A rough deal for Labour ministers Jack Straw and Ed Balls.
explanation.walkthrough: Straw and Balls both pose as Labour cabinet ministers. A yahoo, from Gulliver's Travels, is a coarse brute.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough is a noun for a hooligan or boor, and a yahoo is a crude, uncultured person.

clue.text: Rambler taking turn with slut

parts.note: to wind is to turn, as a road does
bag is a derogatory slang term for a woman

explanation.surface: A hiker going for a walk with a disreputable companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rambler' looks like a walker, but it means someone who talks on and on.
explanation.definitionFit: A rambler in speech is someone who talks at length without point, which is what a windbag does.

clue.text: Lancet to merge with Eye; changes to be made — it could get hot!

indicators.note: making changes means altering the order, so the combined letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written; the Lancet is the medical journal
taken as written; Private Eye, the magazine

explanation.surface: A spoof press report of the Lancet merging with Private Eye, with editorial changes and a heated result.
explanation.definitionFit: Acetylene is a gas that burns at very high temperature in welding torches, so it can certainly get hot.

clue.text: One who's lost faith in Brown? ("Character making U-turn without developing. etc.")

definitions.text: One who's lost faith in Brown?

indicators.note: a U-turn sends you back the way you came, so the character's name runs right to left
without in its old sense of outside means the reversed word wraps round the other letters

parts.note: a character played by an actor is a role

indicators.note: something developing is still taking shape, so the letters that follow are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging

explanation.surface: A disillusioned Labour voter, with a bracketed aside that reads like editorial notes.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed ELOR goes round ECT. Gordon Brown was Prime Minister; a voter who lost faith in him is the kind meant.
explanation.definitionFit: A voter is anyone entitled to choose a government, and the question mark flags that this particular one has turned against Brown.

clue.text: Legislative body that's no stranger to spin

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the upper chamber of Parliament
second meaning: the London cricket ground, which sees plenty of spin bowling

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spin' suggests political spin, but it is cricket. LORD'S is a London cricket ground, the home of the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: The House of Lords makes laws, and Lord's cricket ground regularly hosts spin bowlers turning the ball.

clue.text: Mug shot? Leave behind in jug's receptacle

indicators.note: 'in' places the first word inside the receptacle named after it

parts.note: jugs is slang for breasts, held by a bra cup
to lose something is to leave it behind

explanation.surface: A police photo, then an instruction about what to leave in a container for a jug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jug' looks like a pitcher, but 'jugs' is slang for breasts.
explanation.definitionFit: A mug is slang for a face, so a mug shot can be a photograph filmed from very near the face.

clue.text: Unusual effort needed to comprehend Conservative measure (a bit leftish?)

indicators.note: to comprehend is to take in, so the rearranged letters hold the others
unusual means not in its normal form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
an en is a printer's measure of width

explanation.surface: A political puzzle about a Tory policy that seems slightly left-wing.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged OFFTRE splits to hold C and EN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something slightly off-centre is displaced a little to one side, perhaps to the left; the question mark flags the political pun.

clue.text: Brown, once seeing risk — "turn back!"

parts.note: to chance something is to risk it

indicators.note: turning back means going in the opposite direction, so the word for turn is read backwards

parts.note: a roll is a turn over; reversed it reads LLOR

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown taking a gamble and being warned to retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Brown held the Treasury post for ten years before becoming Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Brown's previous job was Chancellor of the Exchequer, the UK finance minister, so 'once' points to that former office.

clue.text: Fair escape? Eff-off!

indicators.note: 'off' removes the letter named just before it from the word

parts.note: flight is escape, as in taking flight
eff is the spelled-out name of the letter

explanation.surface: A fair getaway, met with a mild swear word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eff off' looks like a euphemistic curse, but it says take away F.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair hair or skin is pale in colour, which is what light means here.

clue.text: see 25ac.
Traditionally macho type but maybe not one whose erection you could depend on?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the rugged hero of the Wild West

definitions.text: maybe not one whose erection you could depend on
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a dodgy tradesman whose buildings may fall down

explanation.walkthrough: 'Erection' tempts a smutty reading, but it is a structure put up by a builder; a cowboy builder is British slang for an unreliable one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the archetypal tough rancher and, in British slang, a shoddy, untrustworthy tradesman.

clue.text: Balls possibly appended to special guests, as underpants usually are

indicators.note: a special version is a custom one, so the letters are arranged in a new way

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging
Ed Balls, Labour politician
surface padding: hints that Balls is a name rather than anatomy

explanation.surface: A smutty image of balls being attached to some visitors, with an underwear punchline.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Balls was a senior Labour minister of the Brown era; 'possibly' warns that Balls is a name, not anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: Underpants normally have a gusset, a reinforcing panel at the crotch, so they are described as gusseted.

clue.text: (& 19ac.) Common people's sweetheart had gun customised

indicators.note: something customised has been altered to order, so the letters are put in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging

explanation.surface: A tabloid line about a commoner's girlfriend with a modified firearm.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The great unwashed is a scornful idiom for the masses, ordinary folk seen from above.

clue.text: A singularly cheeky person would be inadequate

definitions.text: A singularly cheeky person would be inadequate

parts.note: surface: someone notable for insolence
setter's reading: someone with a single buttock, only half a backside

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheeky' suggests impudence, but read literally a person with one cheek has only half a bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: The British slang term means done in a feeble, inadequate way, and literally describes having half a backside.

clue.text: Could be Harriet's task to protect leaders of exhausted party

indicators.note: protecting something means surrounding it, so the task word goes round the other letters

parts.note: a duty is a task you must do

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their opening letters, so only the first of each is kept

parts.note: first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Harriet Harman's job is to shield a tired Labour party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could be Harriet' is a definition by example: Harriet Harman was Labour's deputy leader under Brown.
explanation.definitionFit: Harriet Harman was Labour's deputy leader, so she is an example of a second-in-command, hence 'could be'.

clue.text: Miliband's last to admit hospital places on the decline

indicators.note: 'last' keeps only the final letter of the surname

parts.note: final letter of the surname
to own up is to admit
hospital wards are where patients stay

explanation.surface: A Miliband is finally letting hospitals take patients as standards slide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admit' suggests hospital admissions, but it means to confess.
explanation.definitionFit: Going downwards means heading lower, and something on the decline is sinking in that way.

clue.text: Place former party leader, not Hard Harry

parts.note: PL is the standard abbreviation of place, as in street names

indicators.note: 'not' tells you to leave something out, here the letter standing for hard

parts.note: William Hague, former Conservative leader
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Instructions to seat an ex-party leader somewhere, but not a man called Hard Harry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' reads as part of a name, but it is a verb and the definition. William Hague led the Conservatives from 1997 to 2001.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry someone is to pester and torment them persistently, which is what to plague means.

clue.text: One putting a gloss on broadcast: "Money no longer available"

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard over the air, so the spelling follows the sound

parts.note: a gilder applies gold leaf

explanation.surface: Someone spinning a broadcast about funds that have dried up.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dutch currency was replaced by the euro in 2002.
explanation.definitionFit: The guilder was the Netherlands' currency until the euro arrived, so it is money that can no longer be had.

clue.text: see 14ac.
Not pissed so kept in the film?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: sober, since cut is British slang for drunk
second meaning: not removed by the editor or censor

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' meaning drunk is British slang, so not cut is sober.
explanation.definitionFit: A scene left in a film is not edited out, and someone sober is, in slang, not drunk.

clue.text: Was a confessor given fresh air and drink?

parts.note: to sing is slang for confessing to police

indicators.note: fresh means newly made, so the word that follows is remade in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging

explanation.surface: An informant being rewarded with a breath of fresh air and a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' suggests a tune to sing, but it is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Sangria is a Spanish punch of red wine and fruit, a kind of drink.

clue.text: Transport bill backed by Herb and Bill

indicators.note: something backed has been moved in reverse, so the first word for bill runs right to left

parts.note: AC, account, is a bill; reversed it reads CA
dill is a culinary herb
AC, account, again stands for a bill

explanation.surface: A transport bill getting support from two men called Herb and Bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herb' and 'Bill' pose as men's names, but they are a plant and an account.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cadillac is a luxury American car, an example of a means of transport.

clue.text: Whacks off with Conservative oafs

indicators.note: 'off with' tells you to remove the abbreviation named next

parts.note: clouts are heavy blows
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: Thugs beating up Tories, with a crude hint.
explanation.definitionFit: Louts and oafs are both clumsy, boorish people with no manners.

clue.text: Engineer gets to toss king off with broken leg

indicators.note: taking something off removes it, so the letter standing for king goes

parts.note: British slang for the act, as in 'tosser'
K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: something broken is no longer in its original shape, so these letters get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging

explanation.surface: An injured engineer trying to throw a king off, with a typical Private Eye double entendre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' looks like a person, but it is the verb meaning to contrive.
explanation.definitionFit: To engineer an outcome is to bring it about by cunning, just as to wangle something is to obtain it by scheming.

clue.text: Mistake genital areas for an auditor

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so the answer only needs to sound right

parts.note: the lap is the area across the thighs and groin when seated

explanation.surface: Someone confusing body parts in front of an accountant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' looks like an accountant checking books, but it means a hearer.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapse is a slip or brief failure, which is a kind of mistake.

clue.text: (& 11ac.) Accordingly, remove clothing and beat it

parts.note: so means therefore, accordingly
an old verb for taking a hat or garment from the body

explanation.surface: A curt order to strip and get lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are rude British slang commands telling someone to go away at once.

clue.text: Talk like politician Balls?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to speak complete nonsense, as politicians are said to
second meaning: rubbish, nonsense as an exclamation

explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' poses as Ed Balls, the Labour politician the clue seems to mention, but it is the slang word for rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means complete nonsense; read as verb plus noun it is what a politician is mocked for doing when speaking.

clue.text: Balls' second day shift talk?

indicators.note: 'second' picks out the letter in position two of the preceding word

parts.note: the second letter of the word
D is the abbreviation for day
a shift is a simple straight dress

explanation.surface: Ed Balls giving a speech on the second day of a working shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shift' suggests a work period, but it is a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: An address is a formal speech, a kind of talk given to an audience.

clue.text: Defector case dismissed, being on the piss

indicators.note: a case dismissed is thrown out and scattered, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, before rearranging
pee is another word for urine

explanation.surface: A defector's court case is thrown out while he is out drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the piss' is British slang for a drinking session; here 'on' just places one piece after another.
explanation.definitionFit: A defector flees one side for another, so they are someone who has got away, an escapee.
